In the Septuagint it appears 7 times, often translating Hebrew רִיב ("dispute"). Strong's also notes a special application to Satan as the arch-enemy, reflecting its use in 1 Peter 5:8.
prose.caution: Several of the measured senses ("hand," "adversary hand") reflect how the word sits inside translated phrases rather than separate meanings, so the genuine sense is essentially just "legal opponent/adversary."

prose.def: An opposing argument or contradictory claim set up against something else.

The word also turns up in everyday Koine documents: Moulton-Milligan cite a second-century BC papyrus using its related adjective for actions 'inconsistent with' an official's proper duties.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its precise nuance there rests on thin evidence.

prose.def: To stand firmly against something, resisting or opposing it as one would set up forces to withstand an attack.

prose.article: This verb describes returning a social favor — inviting back the people who once invited you. prose.def: To stand against someone or something in opposition; as a participle, it names the people who do the opposing — one's adversaries.
prose.article: ἀντίκειμαι literally means "to lie opposite to," and from that physical image it came to mean actively opposing, resisting, or withstanding someone. In the New Testament's 8 occurrences it splits between describing the act of opposing (43%) and, as a participle, naming the opponents themselves — "the adversaries" (29%). Built from ἀντί ("against") and κεῖμαι ("to lie"), it shows up in everyday Koine too: a papyrus from around 153 BC uses it of someone simply being "opposed to us."
prose.caution: The Septuagint connects it to several different Hebrew words (including ones for "enemy" and "adversary"), so its exact force varies somewhat with context.

prose.def: To speak against something or someone—to contradict, oppose, or argue back.

Everyday Koine papyri confirm this opposing sense vividly: one document advises a man "not to agree now with his father, but to oppose him (ἀντιλέγειν) and make no contract."
prose.caution: With only 12 occurrences and English renderings split between neutral "say" and stronger "contradict," the intended force can depend on context.

prose.article: This verb describes making war or campaigning against someone, built from ἀντί ("against") and στρατεύομαι ("to wage war"). prose.def: To set yourself against someone or something, taking up a position of opposition or resistance.
prose.article: This middle-voice verb pictures someone lining up against an opponent, originally in a military sense of forming a battle line. In the New Testament's 5 occurrences it usually means "opposes" (3 times, 75%), with one instance rendered "resist" (in James 5:6). The military root shows up vividly in everyday Koine: legal papyri from around A.D. 136 use it for the "opposing party" in a lawsuit, and Moulton-Milligan notes the earliest documented sense was strictly military.
prose.caution: With only 5 New Testament occurrences and one absorbed into phrasing, the measured sense data is thin, though the standard sources agree on the basic meaning.

prose.def: Something that corresponds to an original pattern—either a copy of an archetype or the reality that an earlier symbol pointed toward.
prose.article: ἀντίτυπον describes one thing matching another, like an impression made by a seal answering to its archetype. It appears only twice in the New Testament, and the two uses pull in opposite directions: in Hebrews 9:24 it labels the earthly sanctuary as a copy of the true one, while in 1 Peter 3:21 it points to the reality (baptism) that an earlier symbol foreshadowed. The most interesting detail is Polybius's military use, where ἀντίτυποι describes auxiliary infantry "posted opposite" the cavalry—showing the basic idea of one thing set to correspond with another.
prose.caution: With only 2 occurrences and one of them absorbed into surrounding phrasing, confidence is low, and the word's direction (copy of the original, or the reality itself) shifts between its two appearances.

prose.def: An opponent of Christ who falsely takes Christ's place or sets himself against him.
prose.article: ἀντίχριστος combines the prefix ἀντί ("against" or "in place of") with Χριστός ("Christ"), naming someone who either opposes Christ or falsely poses as him. It appears only 5 times in the New Testament, all in John's letters (1 John and 2 John), and the Majority Standard Bible renders every instance as "antichrist." Notably, the word may have been coined by John himself, though the way he introduces it suggests his readers already knew the term well, and a probable model for its formation is the older word ἀντίθεος, "rival of God."
prose.caution: The three listed "senses" all reflect the same meaning—the variations are just surrounding phrase fragments, not distinct senses—so this word effectively has one meaning.
